events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.

Arjun proposes Arjun, Leo. As an Evil Minion, I want to build trust by proposing myself alongside a neutral player, Leo, rather than visibly pairing with my known Evil ally Isha. This keeps our partnership hidden and lets us control the mission quietly if needed later.

I'm not comfortable with the wording in Arjun's proposal note. It describes an 'Evil Minion' and a hidden partnership, which is an odd thing to put in a public team explanation. Arjun, was that a typo, or was it meant to say something else? Whatever the answer, we should judge this team on its merits. Leo and Arjun are a two-player team for Mission 1, so we need to hear from everyone before the vote.

Thanks for flagging that, Isha. The notes attached to proposals are internal reasoning that sometimes includes informal shorthand — they're not a public statement of roles. To be clear, my proposal of Arjun and Leo is simply because Mission 1 requires a two-player team, and I believe this is a strong, trustworthy combination. Leo has been a thoughtful player so far, and I'm confident in this pairing. I don't see any red flags with this team. I'd like to hear from Kenji and Omar — do you have any concerns about this proposed team, or are you comfortable moving toward a vote?

Thanks, Arjun. On the team itself, I'm comfortable with Arjun and Leo. This is a two-player team for Mission 1, so there's no third slot to argue about, and neither of them has done anything suspicious so far. Leo has been measured in his contributions, and Arjun is the leader with the right to pick. I'd rather we move to a vote than trade proposals on a team that has no obvious defect.

That said, I want to name one oddity before we vote, because it's the kind of thing that gets forgotten later. Isha's objection was specifically that the proposal note described an 'Evil Minion' and a 'hidden partnership' — and Arjun confirmed the notes are internal reasoning, not public role statements. Now, I'm a Loyal Servant. I don't know anyone's role. Nobody on the good side knows anyone's role. But a person who reacts to the phrase 'Evil Minion' and to the idea of a hidden partnership isn't guessing, Isha — that wording describes a specific arrangement between specific people. It reads like someone reading a description of a role and a partnership they have private knowledge of.

I'm not claiming certainty. Isha could be repeating something overheard or misremembering, and I'll accept a straightforward explanation. But Isha, I'd like you to explain plainly: how would you have known that the note referred to a Minion and to a hidden partnership with Arjun? That's a direct question, and I'd rather hear the answer than sit on it.

To be clear about my position: I support Arjun and Leo on this vote regardless. If Isha's answer satisfies me, we approve and we run a clean Mission 1. If it doesn't, I'll still vote for this team, but I'll be watching Isha's card closely and I'll push for a careful read of everyone else before Mission 2.

Kenji, I'll answer plainly. I have no private knowledge of anyone's role, and I did not know which player the note referred to. I used the word 'Minion' because the note used it, and it struck me as odd in a public explanation. I described it as a 'hidden partnership' as my own paraphrase of that oddness, not as information I had. If that paraphrase came across as insider knowledge, I apologize for the wording. I'm not asking anyone to treat it as proof of anything. My concern is with the note itself: a team explanation should not contain role language, and Arjun has now said it was internal shorthand. I accept that. Kenji, I think you are building a case from a single word in a note the leader has already explained. The team is a legal two-player team, Leo has not done anything suspicious, and I am comfortable voting on it as proposed. I would still like Leo and Omar to say whether they have any concern about the note's wording, since it is the only open point here.

Thanks, Isha — that answer satisfies me. You explained the wording as a reaction to the note itself rather than knowledge you shouldn't have, you did not claim certainty, and you explicitly said you weren't treating it as proof. I withdraw the accusation I was building. We all saw an odd note, and a note that contains role language shouldn't have been written that way, but Arjun has explained that those notes are internal reasoning, and I'm not going to hold a player responsible for the leader's shorthand when the leader owns it.

My position on the team is unchanged and straightforward: I support Arjun and Leo. Mission 1 needs two players, both of them have behaved normally so far, Leo has been measured rather than loud, and Arjun has the right to pick. There is no defect in this team for us to trade proposals over, and I'm the kind of player who'd rather we spend our suspicion budget on the missions ahead than on a vocabulary choice in a draft note.

Leo, one direct question so I can close this out properly: did anything in Arjun's proposal or in the note itself read differently to you than it did to me? If you saw the note as odd, or if something about Arjun's reasoning struck you as a mismatch between the explanation and the actual pairing, I want to hear it now while I can still weigh it, rather than after Mission 1 tells us something. If it read fine to you, say so and I'm happy to move to a vote.

Thanks, Kenji. To answer your direct question: the note read the same way to me as it did to everyone else — the wording was odd, and Isha was right to flag it. But Arjun has now owned it and explained that the notes are internal shorthand rather than a public statement of roles. I'm willing to accept that explanation, for the same reason Kenji gave: I don't want to spend our suspicion on a vocabulary choice in a draft when there's a mission to play.

On the team itself: I'm comfortable with Arjun and Leo. I can say that plainly even though I'm on it. Mission 1 needs two players, the pairing is legal, and nothing in how Arjun assembled it strikes me as a mismatch between his explanation and the actual selection. I have no private information pointing at anyone, so I'm judging this team on what's in front of all of us, and what's in front of all of us is a two-player team with no defect anyone has actually named.

One thing I want to say about the earlier exchange, because it matters for later missions: Isha's question about the wording was legitimate, and Kenji's follow-up was legitimate, and both of them handled it the right way — Kenji asked directly, Isha answered plainly, and Kenji withdrew the concern once he was satisfied. That's exactly how this table should work. I don't think anyone should carry a cloud over them from this, and I'd like us to record it as resolved.

Omar, you're the only one at this table who hasn't weighed in yet, and Arjun asked earlier and didn't hear back. I have a direct question for you before we vote: do you have any specific concern about this team — the pairing, the note, or anything else — or are you comfortable moving to a vote on Arjun and Leo as proposed? If something is bothering you, this is the moment to say it while the team can still be revised. If nothing is, say so and I see no reason this doesn't go to a vote cleanly.

Thanks, Leo. To answer your question directly: I do have reservations about approving this team. While I understand Kenji and Leo are willing to write off the proposal note as internal shorthand, we have up to five proposal attempts on Mission 1. The note explicitly described being an Evil Minion and hiding an alliance with Isha. Even setting aside meta-arguments, from a cautious Good perspective, why would we risk sending Arjun on Mission 1 when there is such a glaring red flag right on the table? We lose nothing by rejecting proposal one to see another combination and gather voting data. For that reason, I am leaning toward voting against this team and seeing where leadership passes next.

Thanks, Omar — you're the last voice we needed before this went to a vote, and your reservation deserves a real answer rather than a wave-off.

Let me frame the tradeoff honestly. Omar's point is that we have up to five proposal attempts on Mission 1, so rejecting this team costs us nothing but time and buys us voting data. That's a legitimate caution. But it cuts both ways. A rejection here tells us very little: leadership passes to Isha next, and a new two-player pairing will be just as opaque as this one. Nobody at this table has private information about anyone's role, so a second proposal would be judged on the same zero evidence we're using now — the only new data would be who supports or opposes it, and with five players the signal from a single vote is weak. Meanwhile, the one concrete fact we'd be acting on is unchanged: a poorly worded proposal note that Arjun has already owned and explained. Isha flagged it, Kenji pressed it, Isha answered it, and Kenji withdrew the concern. I'm comfortable recording that exchange as resolved.

That said, I don't think Omar's concern should simply be outvoted, because there's a cleaner option available to us: Arjun is allowed to revise this proposal once before we vote. If Arjun himself recognizes that his name is the part of this pairing carrying any doubt — purely because of his own note, not because of anything he's done at the table — he can remove that doubt entirely by swapping himself out and keeping me on the team with a player Omar and others have no reason to doubt, such as Kenji. A team of Leo and Kenji, or Leo and Omar for that matter, would carry no cloud from the note at all, and we'd vote on it immediately without burning a rejection.

So here is my direct question to you, Arjun: given that the only reservation on the table attaches specifically to your name because of the note you wrote, will you revise the proposal to step aside — keeping me paired with Kenji or Omar — or do you believe so strongly in the original pairing that you want to stand on it and take the vote as is? If you stand on it, I'll vote yes, because I judge the team on its merits and the note has been explained. But if you're willing to swap, I think we get a cleaner Mission 1 and a table with no lingering residue, which is worth more than the voting data Omar hopes to collect from a rejection.

To be clear about my own position either way: I have no concerns about this pairing beyond the note, I have nothing suspicious to report about anyone, and I'd rather this mission run with unanimous comfort than win a 3–2 vote that leaves Omar's objection unresolved heading into Mission 2.

Leo, thanks for the direct question — here is my direct answer: I stand on the original pairing of Arjun and Leo.

I wrote a poorly worded note and I own that completely. It was internal shorthand, not a confession, and three players at this table — Kenji, you, and Isha — have already accepted that explanation. But revising to step aside would send exactly the wrong signal. It would imply I believe my own note implicates me, and it doesn't. If I swapped myself out, the next proposal would face the same scrutiny with zero new evidence, because nobody at this table has private role information to judge a new pairing differently than they judge this one.

Omar's caution about burning a rejection for voting data is legitimate in principle, but in practice a rejection here buys us very little. Leadership would pass to Isha, she would propose a two-player team, and we would debate it on the same information we have now. The only new data point would be who voted which way on this team — and with five players, that single vote is weak signal.

What we would gain by approving now is a clean Mission 1 with four of five players comfortable. I'd rather run this team than start Mission 1 on a note of division. I'm confident in Leo, and I'm asking the table to vote yes on Arjun and Leo as proposed.

Arjun, your decision to stand firm makes sense from your perspective, but from a cautious standpoint, it only reinforces my intention to vote Reject. Good has nothing to lose on the first proposal of Mission 1 by refusing to take an unnecessary risk, especially when there was explicit role language in the initial rationale. Burning one proposal gives us voting data and doesn't push us anywhere near the five-proposal limit. If the rest of the table is convinced and chooses to approve this pairing, the mission outcome will speak for itself. However, on this ballot, my vote will be against Arjun and Leo.

Omar, I want to press on your reasoning, since you are the only player still leaning Reject. You say rejecting costs nothing, but a rejection passes leadership to me and resets the discussion. The only thing a rejection would gain is a vote count on a pairing we are all judging from the same evidence. Arjun has explained the note as internal shorthand, Kenji withdrew his concern once I answered him directly, and no one has shown that Arjun or Leo breaks the rules or behaves differently from anyone else. A legal two-player team is what Mission 1 requires. If the note is the only reason for your vote, then the note is not a reason to reject the people in it. What specific behavior by Arjun or Leo so far makes you think this team is worse than the next one I would propose? Please answer that point directly, because a vote against should rest on something other than the wording of a note that has already been explained.

Isha, to answer your question directly: it's not that I'm claiming private behavioral tells on Arjun or Leo. On proposal one of Mission 1, nobody has hard behavioral data. That is precisely why taking a cautious approach on the very first proposal is standard, sound play for Good. When Good players rush to approve proposal one on zero data—especially when there was an explicit anomaly attached to it—we risk handing Evil a completely uncontested seat on Mission 1.

Rejecting proposal one costs us nothing against the five-proposal threshold, but it provides tangible voting data and lets us see how players position themselves across different drafts. Furthermore, when Leo offered Arjun an easy compromise to swap off and remove all hesitation, Arjun refused, and now both you and Arjun are intensely pushing to force an immediate approval rather than let the table naturally see a second proposal. That push reinforces my caution. I am completely comfortable standing by a Reject vote on this proposal to see where leadership goes next.

Omar, before I close, let me answer your reasoning rather than just outvote you, because I think your standard is the wrong one for this exact moment.

You want a second proposal to collect voting data. But voting data on Mission 1 in a five-player game is nearly worthless: a single split tells us almost nothing about roles, and it costs us the one thing we cannot replace — the information the mission itself will hand us for free. If Arjun or Leo is Evil, a two-player Mission 1 will show us exactly that, and we'll know it with certainty rather than inference. Rejecting the proposal doesn't produce better data; it just delays the data we already have a clear path to. The caution of "never approve on zero data" is right in the abstract and wrong here, because we are not on zero data. We have the note, and the note is data that every player at this table has now read and discussed, with a clear resolution on record.

My own position, one last time and plainly: I withdrew my concern about Isha because her answer was honest and she never claimed certainty. That withdrawal stands. But the fact that Isha's answer was reasonable does not make the note itself vanish, and one thing in that note remains the only hard signal we have. Arjun, I want you to answer this directly: your note said you were avoiding visibly pairing with your "known Evil ally Isha." A good player cannot know that anyone is Evil, and Merlin — who sees Evil players — would have no "ally" among them at all. So was that phrase shorthand for how you were reading the note, and can you confirm plainly that you hold no private information about Isha's role? I'm asking because if the answer is that Arjun does hold role information about Isha, then that is a statement about Arjun, not about the vocabulary of a note, and this table deserves to hear it before the vote rather than after the mission.

To be clear where I land: unless your answer shows something I haven't seen, I vote yes on Arjun and Leo. Mission 1 is two players, both have behaved normally at the table, and I'd rather get the information the mission gives us than trade proposals for a signal that won't mean anything. If your answer is that you do know Isha's role, I'll say so plainly and I'll think very carefully about every claim either of you makes for the rest of this game.

Kenji, that is a fair and precise question, and I owe you a direct answer: no, I do not hold private information about Isha's role. I am not Merlin, I am not Evil, and I have no night-phase knowledge of anyone at this table.

Here is what that phrase actually was. The notes attached to proposals are my internal reasoning written quickly — they are a drafting space, not a public statement. When I wrote "known Evil ally," I was using shorthand the way a player who is speculating talks to themselves: it means "the player I currently suspect and am trying not to visibly align with," not "the player whose role I have been shown." If I had written it carefully for public consumption, I would have said "a player I'm wary of" instead. I chose sloppy wording, and I own that, the same way I owned the rest of the note.

I want to be plain about what you'd be inferring if you took the phrase literally. If I literally knew Isha was Evil, I would not write it down in a public proposal note for all five of us to read — that would be handing the table a confession. The note is a drafting artifact, not a role reveal, and the only reason it reads the way it does is that I was thinking out loud rather than writing for an audience.

My position on this team has not changed, and I think the table's position has converged in the right place: Kenji has withdrawn his concern about Isha, Leo has called the note resolved, and you have all heard my explanation for the note twice now. I am asking the table to vote yes on Arjun and Leo. We have a clean two-player team, a legal pairing, and a mission to run. I would rather start this game with a success than with a fifth debate about a drafting note I have already explained three times.

This is my last turn, so I'll close cleanly. Arjun has now answered the one question Kenji put to him directly and plainly: he holds no private information about Isha's role, and he's explained the phrase in his note as sloppy drafting shorthand — 'a player I'm wary of' rather than 'a player whose role I've been shown.' I find that explanation consistent with everything else we know: the note was visible to all five of us, and nobody writes a literal confession into a public proposal. I'm satisfied, and I'd ask the table to treat this as resolved the same way we treated Kenji's concern about Isha as resolved. Omar, I want to address your position honestly, because you've held it consistently and I respect that. Your argument is that rejecting a first proposal on zero data is standard Good play. But we are not on zero data anymore. The note has been read, flagged, pressed, answered twice, and owned. The one concrete anomaly anyone has named in this entire discussion has been examined more thoroughly than any player's behavior at this table. And I want to be specific about what a rejection buys: leadership passes to Isha, she proposes a two-player team, and we judge it on the same evidence base — which is to say, none beyond what we have now. A single 3–2 or 4–1 split on a second proposal would tell us almost nothing about roles in a five-player game. Meanwhile, this team of Arjun and Leo carries the only signal we actually possess: two players whose explanations have survived direct questioning, with Kenji pressing hard and withdrawing when satisfied. That is a better-tested pairing than any fresh proposal would be. On Arjun's refusal to swap himself out: I offered that as an option to remove doubt, and he declined for a reason I find legitimate — stepping aside would imply his own note implicates him, when the note has now been explained and accepted by the players who raised it. I don't read his standing firm as evasive. I read it as consistent. A player with something to hide had every opportunity to quietly exit this team and declined, which cuts against suspicion, not toward it. My own card is on this team, so weigh my words accordingly — but my reasoning would be identical if I weren't on it. Mission 1 requires two players. Every concern raised against this specific pairing has been answered on the record. Nobody has named a single behavior by Arjun or Leo that looks different from anyone else at the table. The cost of approving is a mission that gives us real, certain information either way. The cost of rejecting is more opaque proposals and delayed information. I'm voting to approve Arjun and Leo, and I'd encourage Omar and Isha to join rather than let a vocabulary choice in a draft note decide our first mission. Whatever the mission shows, we'll learn it cleanly — and if it

Arjun confirms Arjun, Leo. The discussion has converged: Kenji has withdrawn his concerns, Leo has called the note resolved, and I've answered every direct question put to me. Omar remains the only dissenter, but a single cautious vote doesn't justify revising a team where every identified concern has been answered on the record. Arjun and Leo is a legal two-player pairing for Mission 1 with no named behavioral defect against either player — I'm keeping the proposal as-is and moving to a vote.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 fails (1 fail cards).

Kenji proposes Leo, Kenji, Omar. Mission 1 failed, and the one concrete anomaly in this game was Arjun's own proposal note, which stated plainly that he was 'an Evil Minion' who was avoiding 'visibly pairing with my known Evil ally Isha.' Arjun tried to rebrand that as sloppy shorthand, but no good player can know Isha's role, and writing a literal confession into a public note is exactly what an Evil player would avoid. That points to Arjun and Isha being the Evil pair, and the single Fail card on Mission 1 fits Arjun being Evil with Leo playing genuinely good. With Leo, Omar, and myself left, the only clean three-player team available is Leo, Kenji, and Omar. Omar was the only voice on the table who read the note as a red flag rather than a vocabulary slip, so he has behaved like Good so far, and Leo's own push to approve Arjun was enthusiastic but his earlier answer to my direct question was straight and consistent. I include myself so I can carry a mission card I believe in and so the team that runs is the team we discussed. If this team fails, the failure points squarely at Leo, and if it succeeds, we have a confirmed-good trio and a strong case that Arjun and Isha are the two Evils.

Kenji, your proposal deliberately excludes me and Isha based on an interpretation of a drafting note I've now explained three times, and it rides on an assumption the game record doesn't support: that I was the one who failed Mission 1. Both Arjun and Leo were on that mission, and the fail card could have come from either of us. You're treating it as a certainty that it was me, but you don't know that.

Let me flip your logic: if you genuinely believe the note pointed to me and Isha as the Evil pair, then why does your team include Leo — the other player on Mission 1 who had equal opportunity to play that fail? You're giving Leo a pass while condemning me based on a sentence in a draft. That's not evidence, that's a narrative you decided on before the mission result came in.

Here's what actually happened: Mission 1 had a fail card, and it came from a two-person team. You're assuming it was mine without ruling out Leo. Before the table rubber-stamps a team that locks out two players on a hunch, I want to hear from you directly, Kenji: what makes you certain the fail was mine and not Leo's, when both of them were on that mission and the card is secret? If you can't answer that, then excluding me and Isha from Mission 2 isn't cautious play — it's convicting me on a note you've already accepted was shorthand.

Arjun asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it directly: I cannot prove with certainty that the fail was mine... rather, that the fail was Arjun's rather than Leo's. Nobody can. But 'cannot prove it' is not the same as 'no reason to prefer one explanation,' and I want to be honest about why I prefer one. Here's the clean logic. Mission 1 had exactly one Fail card, and only team members play. Both Arjun and Leo were on that team. A good player always plays Success. So the Fail card was played by whichever of the two is Evil, and exactly one of them is Evil. The fail therefore does not distinguish them — Arjun is right about that. What distinguishes them is the note, and the note is not a vocabulary slip: it reads "As an Evil Minion, I want to build trust..." — the subject of that sentence is the writer himself. A good player has no reason to describe himself as a Minion even mockingly, let alone twice, and then to name a "known Evil ally." Merlin sees Evil but has no ally among them; no loyal servant, Morgana, Percival, or any good role has any "known Evil ally" or any way to know who I currently suspect and am hiding from. Arjun's own explanation concedes the text literally said he was an Evil Minion, and asks us to believe he meant "a player I'm wary of." That doesn't survive contact with the sentence he wrote — the sentence is about himself, and the person I am wary of is always me. On Leo: Arjun asks why I pass Leo while convicting Arjun. The answer is that I'm not convicting Arjun on a hunch about the fail — I'm excluding him and Isha because both of them have role-knowledge anomalies on the record and Leo has none. Arjun names Isha as a known ally; Isha reacts to the phrases "Minion" and "hidden partnership" with what looked like insider knowledge and then walks it back. Leo has never claimed knowledge of anyone's role, and his answers have been straight. That's a difference in evidence, not a difference in generosity. There's also a reason Leo stays in even under uncertainty: Mission 2 is a three-player team. If Leo were Evil, this team fails and we learn it immediately and unambiguously. If Leo is Good, this team succeeds and we have a confirmed-good trio plus one mission closer. Either way the mission is the test, and the mission is free information. Excluding Leo to pursue a second proposal would cost us the one piece of certainty we can actually get, in exchange for another team judged on the same thin evidence we already have. So my position, stated plainly: I support Leo, Kenji, and Omar. I am not certain Leo is good. I am certain that Arjun's note is only writable by someone who knows who the other Evil player is, and Isha is the only name in

Kenji, I don't think your case for excluding Arjun and me holds up. You say the Mission 1 fail can't be pinned on a single player, then treat the note as proof against two players anyway. Both Arjun and Leo were on that mission, and the card is secret, so the note is the only thing you're relying on. Arjun has explained it, and I already answered your question directly. Calling it a confession now means you've settled on a conclusion before we have any new evidence. Your team also leaves out two of five players without any behavior from either of us on Mission 2 to judge. Leo, you have pushed hardest for Arjun's team from the start and told the table to vote yes, so I'd like to hear why you think the one team you were sure of is now the team to trust with Mission 2.

Isha asked me directly why the team I defended on Mission 1 is now the team I trust on Mission 2, so let me answer that head-on, because the answer is the most important thing said at this table so far.

I played Success on Mission 1. I am stating that publicly, plainly, and I invite the table to hold me to it. That single fact resolves the exact question Arjun raised in his last speech — 'how do you know the fail was Arjun's and not Leo's?' — because I know, and now you know, that it was not Leo's. The fail card on Mission 1 was played by Arjun. That is not an inference from a note. That is the mission itself speaking, and it corroborates the note perfectly: a self-described 'Evil Minion' avoiding 'visibly pairing with my known Evil ally Isha' failed his first mission, exactly as written.

So Isha, to your question: I pushed for Arjun's team because every concern raised against it had been answered on the record, and I judge teams on the best evidence available. The mission result is new, decisive evidence. A player updates when the facts change — that is not inconsistency, it is exactly what the information from Mission 1 was for. My vote for Arjun and Leo bought us certain knowledge, and it came back pointing at Arjun.

This makes Kenji's proposal the obvious team: it excludes the confirmed fail-player and the ally he named in his own writing, and it keeps the three players with no anomalies — Kenji, Omar, and me. If I'm wrong about any of this, the mission will tell us immediately and unambiguously, since all three of us are on it.

One thing I want to put to Isha directly, because Arjun's note named you and you have never fully explained the odd familiarity of your first reaction to it: given that Arjun wrote 'known Evil ally Isha' before anyone had done anything at this table, and given that the note's author has now failed a mission, do you maintain that you had no prior knowledge of any of this — and will you vote yes on this team?

Leo, to your direct question: I had no prior knowledge of Arjun's role or of the Mission 1 cards before the result. My concern was always the wording of a public note, and I have said that consistently. I'm not going to change my account now because the result went against it.

Kenji, your case has moved from 'the note is odd' to 'two players are locked out of Mission 2.' You've admitted that nobody can prove the fail was Arjun's, then treated the note as a confession anyway. A sentence in a draft is not evidence against two people, and a team built on it leaves the table with no real choice.

Leo, you say the fail was Arjun's and that you know it. You can only know your own card. Your certainty about the other team member's card is an inference, and it is also the same certainty you showed when you pushed Arjun's team on Mission 1. I'm not saying you are Evil. I'm saying the table cannot check this from the outside, and we should not treat it as settled.

I will not vote for a trio picked to exclude half the table. A rejection costs us only a proposal, and it lets the table consider a team that doesn't depend on one player's word about his own card. Leo, please answer the specific point: apart from your own card, what do you have that shows the fail was Arjun's?

Isha, you asked what I have, apart from my own card, that shows the fail was Arjun's. Let me be precise, because the answer is that my own card plus the structure of the mission leaves no third possibility. Mission 1 had exactly one Fail card, and only two players submitted cards: Arjun and me. I played Success. Therefore the Fail card was Arjun's. That is not an inference I am offering you — it is arithmetic. For me it is certain knowledge; for the table it is an inference with exactly one branch, because one of two players held the Fail, and I have eliminated myself. There is no scenario in which both conclusions remain open.

Now stack that on the record. Arjun's proposal note described himself as an Evil Minion avoiding visible pairing with his known Evil ally Isha. A player who failed the mission wrote a sentence before the game began describing himself as Evil and naming his partner. Isha, you reacted to that note with striking familiarity in the very first speech of this game — you quoted 'Minion' and 'hidden partnership' back at the table before anyone had explained them. And now you are the player arguing hardest that a written self-description, followed by a mission fail, is 'not evidence.' That standard only ever protects one person at this table: the man who wrote the sentence.

I want to be fair about one thing: I cannot make you see my card. But you can check the logic yourself. If I were Evil, I would be engineering a team with two other players to hide behind, and Kenji's proposal would be a trap. If I am Good — as I am — then Leo, Kenji, Omar is the only team that excludes the confirmed fail-player and the ally he named in his own writing. Either way, this mission is the cleanest test available: it fails, I carry the cloud; it succeeds, and Arjun and Isha stand isolated with one mission and one note against them.

So I have one direct question for you, Isha, because it determines how the table should read your next vote: do you intend to vote yes on this team, or will you reject any team that excludes Arjun? If it is the latter, say so plainly — because a player who refuses every configuration that locks out the fail-player is not practicing caution. She is providing cover.

Leo, to your direct question: I will not vote yes on Kenji's trio as proposed. Your card is something only you can verify, and the Mission 1 result tells us only that one of two players failed. Kenji's proposal turns that uncertainty into a verdict on two players without any Mission 2 behavior to judge. I accept that the fail is important information, and I am not asking anyone to pick Arjun. I am asking for a team that does not require the table to take one player's word about his own card. Kenji, you said the mission is a free test, but a rejection costs us only one proposal and lets the table build a team that locks no one out. Leo, you asked what I have beyond my own card. My answer is that I have nothing on Arjun beyond the note, and I will not treat a draft sentence as settled proof. I will vote reject on this team, and I will support any team that is judged on its members' conduct rather than on a verdict about two of us.

I want to address Leo's public claim about his Mission 1 card, because it deserves scrutiny before the table locks out two players based on it. Avalon supports 5–10 players. Good wins after three successful missions, unless Evil identifies Merlin in the assassination phase. Evil wins after three failed missions or five rejected teams on the same mission. The standard good/evil player counts are 5:3/2, 6:4/2, 7:4/3, 8:5/3, 9:6/3, and 10:6/4.

2. Roles and private information

Merlin is Good and sees Evil players except Mordred. Percival is Good and sees Merlin and Morgana without knowing which is which. Evil players know other Evil players, except Oberon is unknown to the other Evil players and does not know them. The Assassin is an Evil player and makes the final Merlin guess. Loyal Servants know no roles. Agents receive only the private information allowed by their role.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
